principal_agent.label: Principal-agent problem / asymmetric information between owners and managers

stages.name: Bounded rationality and satisficing
stages.title: Bounded rationality and satisficing
stages.sub: Why real managers settle for 'good enough' instead of the perfect answer.

steps.q: A manager is asked to pick the single best price for a new product out of thousands of possible prices, by tomorrow morning, using sales data she hasn't fully read yet. Can she actually work out the one perfect answer in time?
steps.right: No, she cannot process it all in time
steps.wrong: Yes, if she works hard enough
steps.hint: Think about how much data, time and brainpower true perfection would need.

steps.q: Given she can't gather and process everything perfectly, what does this do to her ability to make the textbook 'fully rational, optimal' decision?
steps.right: It limits how rational her decision can be
steps.wrong: It has no effect, she can still optimise
steps.hint: The rationality assumption imagines unlimited time and information. Does she have that?
steps.pre: This limit on information, time and mental capacity is called

steps.q: This manager's decision also has to keep shareholders happy about profit, staff happy about pay, and customers happy about quality, all at once. Can one single decision fully satisfy all of them at their maximum?
steps.right: No, she must balance competing demands
steps.wrong: Yes, one decision can maximise all of them
steps.hint: Can shareholders' wish for higher profit and workers' wish for higher pay both be pushed to their maximum at the same time?

steps.q: Given she cannot process every option and cannot fully please every group, what kind of price is she realistically aiming for: the mathematically perfect one, or one that works reasonably well for everyone?
steps.right: One that works reasonably well for everyone
steps.hint: If perfection is out of reach, what's the realistic target?
steps.pre: Aiming for an acceptable outcome across several goals, rather than the perfect one, is called

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: This manager works for owners who cannot watch her every move and don't know everything she knows about the market. If she can't be sure what they'd choose in her position, and can't process every option anyway, is 'good enough' or 'perfect' the sensible target for her to report back with?
steps.right: 'Good enough', given what she knows and can check
steps.wrong: 'Perfect', since owners expect the ideal answer
steps.hint: Think about her own limits plus the gap between what she knows and what the owners know.
steps.pre: Bounded rationality, competing stakeholder demands, and the gap between owners and managers together explain why firms pursue
